description: Hi, I am Piyush, 2nd year CSE (AI/ML) student at Polaris School of Technology, Bengaluru. I build AI and full-stack projects. We are doing the Martian Map challenge: a layered Mars route map with hazards, safe paths and science stops from NASA data. Looking for: frontend/maps, UI/UX, GIS or satellite data, and pitching skills. No need to be an expert, just be curious and ready to build!
summary: TARS on Mars is a walking route planner for astronauts on Mars. You pick a base and up to six stops inside Jezero crater, and it finds the safest walking route on the 1 m HiRISE height map. Each kind of ground has its own slope limit (sand 10 degrees, delta fan 15, rock 20), so steep or soft ground is avoided. For every plan it shows the walking time, the oxygen used against your reserve, the point of no return, sun and shadow, radio contact with base, radiation dose, and typical weather for that season and hour. It also suggests science stops at mineral patches you can reach and return from on your oxygen. We checked the map against the real drive of the Perseverance rover: 98.6% of its path inside our map is GO under a single 20 degree slope limit. The same planner also runs on the NASA LOLA map of the Moon's south pole.
details:
Try it live: https://tars-on-mars.vercel.app (a plan takes around 15 seconds on our small free server).

What it does: an astronaut sets a base, stops, oxygen, reserve and walking speed. The planner picks the best stop order and the safest path, then shows time, oxygen, the point of no return (the last spot where you can still walk home on your oxygen), sun and shadow, radio blackouts, radiation dose, climb and descent, and a 3D view of the walk. It can suggest science stops at mineral patches, and it can re-plan when a helicopter scout reports a spot as blocked.

How it works: we turn the 1 m HiRISE height map of Jezero into slope and roughness, mark every square GO, CAUTION or NO-GO using slope limits for each ground type from the USGS geologic map, and search for the lowest-risk path. Weather is the typical value for that season and hour from Perseverance MEDA data. It is not a live feed. Planning works only inside our mapped box.

Checks: 98.6% of Perseverance's real path inside our map is GO under a single 20 degree limit, and 95.2% under our stricter on-foot limits. On the Moon site our slopes agree with NASA's own LOLA slope map on 99.999% of 10.2 million squares. The project has 179 backend tests and 111 frontend tests.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, numpy, scipy, scikit-image, rasterio, pyproj, React, Leaflet, three.js, Vite.

AI use: we built the code and the slide layout with an AI coding assistant. The team chose the idea and the NASA data sources, set the safety rules and limits, directed the build, and reviewed and tested the results.
